Eggs of the Northern fulmar are incubated at a target temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C], though considerable variability is observed under natural nesting conditions. The incubation period itself is relatively protracted, with hatching occurring after approximately 55 days [ab = approximately 55 days] when the egg is maintained at 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. Newly hatched chicks emerge with a modest wet weight of roughly 65 grams [Wwb = roughly 65 grams], reflecting the energetic constraints of yolk provisioning within a calcareous shell. This initial mass is quite low compared to the body sizes these birds will ultimately achieve. The chick, a semi-precocial nestling, depends entirely on biparental provisioning during its early development. Field records show that the period of rapid mass gain is sustained by frequent meals of regurgitated oil and fish delivered by both parents. The nestling stage is energetically demanding, and survival is strongly tied to the consistency of food delivery from the attending adults. During this phase, the downy chick remains brooded within the cliff-side nest scrape, gradually developing the plumage and thermoregulatory capacity needed for eventual independence.

The initial wet weight of the egg before incubation onset is approximately 98 grams [Ww0 = approximately 98 grams], a value that reflects the substantial energy reserve allocated to the embryo within a calcareous shell. This initial mass, combined with the subsequent parental investment during incubation, underpins the growth trajectory of the semi-precocial nestling. The age at which a young fulmar reaches fledging is known to fall between 49 and 58 days, with a typical value of 53 days after hatching [tx = 53 days after hatching] reported in studies of colonies breeding at temperate latitudes at a temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C]. This developmental milestone is achieved under the thermal conditions characteristic of an adult's active metabolic state, specifically a body temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C]. Upon fledging, the young bird departs the nest site and becomes entirely independent of its parents, a stark transition from the intensive provisioning of the nestling phase. The achievement of sustained flight marks the onset of the juvenile period, during which the immature bird must learn to forage over vast oceanic distances without any parental guidance. Post-fledging dispersal can take juveniles hundreds of kilometers from their natal colony. This extended period of learning and exploration is a critical phase in the life cycle, as survival during the first year at sea is thought to be low. The fledgling, now a fully feathered juvenile, faces the considerable challenge of locating patchily distributed prey in a dynamic marine environment.

Sexual maturation in this species does not occur rapidly; instead, the onset of gonadal activity is delayed well beyond the fledging period. Field surveys and long-term mark-recapture studies indicate that puberty is reached at approximately 159 days after hatching [tp = approximately 159 days after hatching] when measured at a core body temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C]. This relatively late attainment of reproductive maturity is consistent with the slow life-history pace observed among many procellariiform seabirds, a group characterized by extended pre-reproductive periods and low annual fecundity. The interval between fledging and the onset of gametogenesis represents a period of continued somatic growth and the accumulation of body condition necessary for future reproductive effort. Immature birds spend these months ranging widely across the North Atlantic, building the energy reserves and foraging proficiency required to support the high costs of egg production and chick rearing. The acquisition of a breeding territory and a mate typically follows the achievement of physiological maturity, though competition for nesting sites on crowded cliff ledges can further delay actual breeding.

First reproduction does not typically occur immediately upon reaching puberty. Instead, the first successful breeding event is commonly deferred until roughly 1,095 days after hatching [tR = roughly 1,095 days after hatching], a timing estimate based on data from similar-sized petrel species, assessed at the standard active body temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C]. This significant delay between physiological maturity and actual first breeding is a well-documented feature of long-lived seabirds, where inexperience, energetic constraints, and intense competition for limited nesting ledges all contribute to deferred breeding. During this interval, young adults engage in prospecting behaviors, visiting colonies and interacting with established breeders. The initial breeding attempts of inexperienced birds often fail, as they lack the refined provisioning skills of older pairs. Annual reproductive output is low, with females producing a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch] and typically only one clutch each year [F_R_i = one clutch each year], representing a maximum reproductive rate consistent with extreme longevity. These life-history traits, including the deferred age at first reproduction and the slow pace of breeding, are balanced by a remarkably extended lifespan.

The maximum lifespan recorded for the Northern fulmar in the wild is remarkably long, with the oldest documented individuals reaching 51 years [am = 51 years], a longevity assessed at a core body temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C]. Such an extended lifespan is characteristic of the order Procellariiformes, a group known for its extremely slow-paced life history. Adult body mass is sexually dimorphic, with fully grown females typically attaining an ultimate wet weight of 706 grams [Wwi = 706 grams], while males are substantially larger, reaching an adult body mass of approximately 884 grams [Wwi = approximately 884 grams]. The initial wet weight of a newly hatched chick is around 98 grams [Ww0 = around 98 grams], a figure that highlights the rapid and dramatic mass increase required to achieve adult dimensions. This growth trajectory, from an initial mass of less than a hundred grams to an adult mass nearly ten times greater in males, is sustained by the lipid-rich diet of regurgitated fish oil and crustaceans. This pattern of extreme longevity, low reproductive output, substantial sexual size dimorphism, and deferred maturity forms a cohesive life-history syndrome that reflects adaptation to the unpredictable food resources of the pelagic marine environment.
